hook: Ms. Brennan, 79, notices her heart fluttering while she gardens. At the clinic, a nurse places ten sticky electrodes on her chest, wrists and ankles. Within a minute the printout shows the problem: no P waves at all, just a wobbling line, and QRS complexes spaced with no pattern. Her atria are no longer contracting in step, and blood pooling there could form a clot.

prereq.q: Which structure normally sets the heart's rate?
prereq.why: The SA node's pacemaker potential climbs fastest, so it reaches threshold first and resets every slower pacemaker.

prereq.q: Why does the signal pause at the AV node for about 0.1 second?
options: AV node cells are small, joined by few gap junctions, and have slow calcium-driven upstrokes
The AV node is several centimeters long
The vagus nerve holds the signal until the atria are empty
prereq.why: The AV node conducts at only about 0.05 meters per second because of its small cells, few gap junctions and slow calcium-driven upstrokes.

prereq.q: During the plateau of a ventricular muscle cell's action potential, the cell is:
prereq.why: During the plateau, Ca²⁺ entering through L-type channels balances K⁺ leaving, so the cell stays depolarized near 0 mV for about 0.2 second.

anatomy.caption: Where the 10 electrodes of a standard 12-lead ECG are placed: each wrist and ankle, and six across the chest.

chain.cause: The SA node fires and a wave of depolarization spreads across both atria.
chain.effect: Current flows between depolarized and resting atrial muscle, and the skin electrodes record the P wave.

chain.cause: The signal reaches the AV node, which conducts slowly.
chain.effect: Almost no muscle is changing voltage, so the trace is flat: the PR segment.

chain.cause: The signal races through the bundle branches and Purkinje fibers into the large ventricular muscle mass.
chain.effect: The ventricles depolarize within about 0.1 second, drawing the tall, narrow QRS complex; atrial repolarization is hidden inside it.

chain.cause: Every ventricular cell is now in its plateau, at about the same voltage.
chain.effect: No current flows between regions, so the trace is flat again: the ST segment.

chain.cause: Ventricular cells repolarize, spread out over time.
chain.effect: The broad T wave appears, and the trace returns to baseline until the next P wave.

misconception.wrong: An ECG shows how well the heart is pumping.
misconception.right: An ECG records only the heart's electrical activity. Contraction usually follows each electrical event, but the ECG cannot show it. A patient can have organized P waves, QRS complexes and T waves on the monitor and still have no pulse, because the muscle is not pumping effectively. To check pumping, you feel for a pulse.

summary: The electrocardiogram (ECG or EKG) records, from the skin, the summed voltage changes of the heart; each lead is one view, and depolarization moving toward a lead's positive electrode draws an upward deflection. The P wave is atrial depolarization, the QRS complex is ventricular depolarization (hiding atrial repolarization), and the T wave is ventricular repolarization. The PR interval, 0.12 to 0.20 second, is mostly AV nodal delay; the flat ST segment is the ventricular plateau; the QT interval spans the ventricular action potential. On paper running at 25 mm per second, rate = 300 ÷ large squares between beats. Arrhythmias include tachycardia (above 100), bradycardia (below 60), first-, second- and third-degree heart block, atrial fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation, which is treated by defibrillation. An artificial pacemaker fires when the heart's own rate is too slow.
